title: The Return to Writing
author: Stephany Anderson, Ed. D.
summary: Stephany Anderson argues that students do not need to master the essay as a single form, but they do need the underlying skills of developing an idea, organizing thought, supporting a claim and communicating to an unfamiliar reader, which every product from podcast to poster depends on. She contends that writing has slipped out of secondary classrooms along with reading, and that handing the problem to the English department fails because history, science, English and mathematics each use words like evidence in different ways. Common frameworks such as Claim, Evidence, Reasoning, Source give students a useful entry point, but become a rigid box if they are never loosened as expertise grows. She distinguishes private writing to learn from polished writing that expresses knowledge, and says schools assign the second without room for the first. The piece closes with practical moves: slowing down around small pieces of text, structured reflection prompts, organizers that mirror the thinking required, and teaching students to argue against their own claims. Her conclusion is that whole-school consistency and disciplinary literacy are partners, not rivals.
points: The word evidence means different things in history, science, English and mathematics, so identical instructions across classrooms can read to students as three different sets of rules.
A common writing framework such as CERS should be a doorway into disciplinary thinking and should be relaxed or complicated as students gain expertise, not become the building itself.
Writing to learn is private and exploratory and should come before writing that crafts an expression of knowledge for an audience, yet schools usually assign only the second.
Graphic organizers should mirror the intellectual work of the task, so the Venn diagram is a poor tool for sustained comparison compared with aligned note frames.
Teachers can make their invisible disciplinary expertise audible by modelling the questions they ask and by teaching students to build counterarguments as a habit of inquiry.
quotes: Students need to know how to develop an idea, organize their thinking, support a claim, and communicate with someone who does not already know what they mean. Sometimes that is done in an essay.
A polished video cannot compensate for unclear thinking, just as an attractive poster cannot make weak evidence convincing.
From an adult perspective, these instructions may sound consistent. From the student’s perspective, they may be three different sets of rules hiding behind the same word.
But a framework is supposed to help someone build. It is not supposed to become the building.
Shared terminology should be a doorway into disciplinary thinking, not the final destination. Whole-school consistency and disciplinary literacy don’t compete.
Polished writing cannot emerge from thinking that has not had room to develop.
The structure of the organizer should mirror the intellectual work they are being asked to do and create a bridge into the writing that follows.

Writing across the disciplines is not about turning every teacher into an English teacher. It is about inviting every teacher to become more explicit about how people in their discipline ask questions, build knowledge, challenge ideas, and communicate what they know.
